stem: A 34-year-old man admitted last night for opioid use disorder asks to start buprenorphine right away — 'I don't want to get sick.' His last heroin use was about 6 hours ago. He is anxious but has no yawning, rhinorrhea, mydriasis, or piloerection; his COWS score is 4. Best next step?
options: A. Start buprenorphine now, before the withdrawal becomes severe | B. Continue serial COWS scoring and start buprenorphine once objective withdrawal is present (COWS roughly 8 to 12) | C. Give a benzodiazepine to control the withdrawal symptoms | D. Reassure him that opioid withdrawal is not dangerous and defer any medication
answer_text: Continue serial COWS scoring and start buprenorphine once objective withdrawal is present (COWS roughly 8 to 12)
why: Comfort-first induction is the trap the request invites — buprenorphine started before objective withdrawal precipitates the withdrawal it was meant to prevent. Serial COWS scores make the timing objective: induction begins at roughly 8 to 12, not at the patient's anxiety. The benzodiazepine belongs to alcohol and sedative withdrawal, and 'not dangerous' is not a plan when MOUD linkage is the discharge intervention.
pearl: Do not start buprenorphine until objective withdrawal is on board (COWS roughly ≥ 8 to 12) or you may precipitate withdrawal.
evidence: t_sud.md 'Acute inpatient management' — begin buprenorphine induction only once objective withdrawal is present (roughly COWS ≥ 8 to 12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal from displacing residual full agonist too early.

stem: A family meeting is held the day before planned discharge for a 52-year-old man admitted after a suicide attempt by overdose. When the agenda reaches safety and warning signs, his wife says: 'We'll keep a close eye on him. And you don't need to worry about the guns — he would never use them, and they're put away.' The attending invites your input. Which response is best?
options: A. 'It makes sense that everyone is exhausted and scared. Before discharge, who can confirm that the firearms — and any stockpiled medications — are actually secured, and how will we know it's done?' | B. 'Firearms are involved in about half of US suicides and are lethal in 85 to 90 percent of attempts — "put away" isn't good enough.' | C. 'That's reassuring — we'll document that the family will keep him safe and that the guns are secured.' | D. 'Discharge can't move forward unless you agree to remove every firearm from the home today.'
answer_text: 'It makes sense that everyone is exhausted and scared. Before discharge, who can confirm that the firearms — and any stockpiled medications — are actually secured, and how will we know it's done?'
why: The best response validates first, stays inside the student role, and converts 'put away' into a concrete, verifiable step — who secures the items and how the team will know. Quoting lethality statistics at the family is the righting reflex in evidence clothing; accepting reassurance leaves means safety unconfirmed at the exact moment risk peaks; and an ultimatum makes the family responsible for treatment while overstepping the student's role.
pearl: Means safety is a lethality intervention, not a formality — 'who can confirm items are secured before discharge?' is a clinical act.
evidence: exp_family.md 'Why It Matters' — documented lethal-means assessment was associated with fewer suicide attempts and deaths at 180 days (0.83% vs 3.3%; Boggs et al. 2020, quasi-experimental); suicide risk peaks in the first week post-discharge (Chung et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017).

stem: A 76-year-old woman on hospital day 3 after hip-fracture repair is referred to psychiatry for 'depression.' She is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeps much of the day; her nurse notes she was conversational yesterday evening but is 'flat' this morning. She cannot recite the months of the year backward. Most likely explanation?
options: A. Major depressive episode — recommend starting an antidepressant | B. Early dementia unmasked by hospitalization | C. Hypoactive delirium — screen for precipitating causes and deliriogenic medications | D. Expected postoperative fatigue — reassure the team and sign off
answer_text: Hypoactive delirium — screen for precipitating causes and deliriogenic medications
why: Acute onset, a course that fluctuates across one shift, and failed months-backward — inattention, the cardinal deficit — assemble the CAM picture; low arousal makes it hypoactive delirium, the form most often mislabeled as depression or overlooked because the patient is quiet. Dementia declines over months, not shifts, and 'postoperative fatigue' does not take attention with it. The work now is finding the drivers — infection, metabolic derangement, deliriogenic medications, retention, constipation, pain.
pearl: Hypoactive delirium is the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, and easily mislabeled as depression.
evidence: delirium.md 'Recognize and screen' — Confusion Assessment Method (CAM, Inouye et al.): acute onset and fluctuating course, plus inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is admitted for a severe depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation. The intern plans to start sertraline today. Before initiating an antidepressant, the most important step is which of the following?
options: A. Start sertraline now — the diagnosis of major depressive disorder is established by her current presentation | B. Obtain a collateral history and formally screen for any prior manic or hypomanic episode before prescribing an antidepressant | C. Start sertraline and add lithium prophylactically to cover any occult bipolar risk | D. Start sertraline and a PRN benzodiazepine, since anxiety commonly accompanies depression
answer_text: Obtain a collateral history and formally screen for any prior manic or hypomanic episode before prescribing an antidepressant
why: Antidepressant before bipolar screen is the key trap: an SSRI started in unrecognized bipolar disorder can trigger mania or rapid cycling. Obtaining collateral and screening for past mania or hypomania is the gatekeeping step before any antidepressant is written. Prophylactic lithium without a diagnosis is premature polypharmacy, and the reflexive benzodiazepine adds risk without resolving the diagnostic question.
pearl: Screen every depressed patient for past mania before writing for an antidepressant.
evidence: t_mood.md 'High-yield pearls' — Screen every depressed patient for past mania before writing for an antidepressant.

stem: A 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium maintenance for two years, presents with a 2-day course of worsening tremor, confusion, and vomiting. Five days ago he began ibuprofen for back pain. Which of the following best explains his presentation?
options: A. A breakthrough manic episode — agitation and confusion signal mood destabilization | B. Viral encephalitis — the confusion warrants urgent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture | C. Serotonin syndrome — lithium combined with ibuprofen triggers excess serotonin activity | D. Lithium toxicity precipitated by ibuprofen reducing renal lithium clearance
answer_text: Lithium toxicity precipitated by ibuprofen reducing renal lithium clearance
why: Treat the number not the patient, Missing the interaction, and Wrong toxidrome are the traps. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window; NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal clearance and push lithium levels into the toxic range — a textbook drug interaction. The 2-day picture of tremor, confusion, and vomiting in a lithium-maintained patient who just started an NSAID is lithium toxicity until proven otherwise.
pearl: NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push lithium levels toward toxicity — check the list when lithium patients deteriorate.
evidence: t_mood.md 'Lithium' — lithium runs a narrow therapeutic window (~0.6–1.2 mEq/L); NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration push levels toward toxicity.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is admitted for new-onset paranoid ideation, disorganized behavior, and auditory hallucinations. Her chart notes she was started on high-dose prednisone three weeks ago for an autoimmune flare. Before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis, the most important step is which of the following?
options: A. Take a thorough medication and medical history and consider a substance- or medication-induced cause before labeling this a primary psychotic disorder | B. Start a second-generation antipsychotic immediately — symptom control should not await diagnostic clarity | C. Diagnose schizophreniform disorder based on symptom type and the absence of a prior psychiatric history | D. Reassure the family that first-episode psychosis in young adults is almost always primary and will respond to antipsychotics
answer_text: Take a thorough medication and medical history and consider a substance- or medication-induced cause before labeling this a primary psychotic disorder
why: Psychosis = schizophrenia is the trap in two forms: treating immediately or diagnosing before excluding secondary causes. Psychosis is a syndrome with a broad differential — corticosteroids are a recognized cause of secondary psychosis, and the clinical picture (new-onset, no prior history, active steroid course) demands a medical workup first. Face-value reassurance skips that step and commits to a prognosis without a diagnosis.
pearl: Psychosis is a syndrome — exclude delirium, substances, medications, and autoimmune causes before settling on a primary disorder.
evidence: t_psychosis.md 'Differential and can't-miss mimics' — Always exclude secondary/medical psychosis before settling on a primary disorder. Screen for substance-induced causes (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, withdrawal) and any medical or medication cause; corticosteroids are a recognized secondary cause (general clinical principle, not individually named on this source page). Do not miss autoimmune/limbic encephalitis.

stem: A 37-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on haloperidol 5 mg/day and sertraline 100 mg/day for a comorbid depressive episode. His sertraline was increased to 150 mg two days ago. He now presents with fever (38.9°C), agitation, diaphoresis, and muscle rigidity. CK is mildly elevated at 680 U/L. The differential includes serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Which finding, if present on examination, would most strongly support serotonin syndrome over neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: A. Uniform lead-pipe resistance throughout the passive range of motion of the upper and lower extremities, with normal deep tendon reflexes. | B. Creatine kinase (CK) above 5,000 U/L with rising creatinine suggesting early rhabdomyolysis. | C. Gradual onset of rigidity and fever developing over 48–72 hours after the haloperidol was started three months ago, with no change in the serotonergic regimen. | D. Ankle clonus with brisk, brisker-than-baseline deep tendon reflexes throughout the lower extremities.
answer_text: Ankle clonus with brisk, brisker-than-baseline deep tendon reflexes throughout the lower extremities.
why: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia → SS. The three distractors all describe NMS features: lead-pipe rigidity (A), dramatically elevated CK (B), and subacute onset tied to the dopamine blocker rather than the serotonergic change (C). Ankle clonus with lower-extremity hyperreflexia (D) is the hallmark physical finding of serotonin syndrome — it reflects serotonin-mediated hyperactivation of spinal reflex arcs and is absent in NMS, where rigidity comes from central dopaminergic dysfunction. The added clinical clues — onset after the sertraline increase, mild rather than dramatic CK — also favor SS over NMS. In practice, both syndromes require stopping the offending agent; the physical exam reflex pattern is the fastest bedside discriminator.
pearl: NMS vs. SS at the bedside: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia → NMS (dopamine blocker, subacute onset); clonus + hyperreflexia → SS (serotonergic agent, rapid onset hours).
evidence: psychotic_disorders_inpatient_teaching.md 'Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs. serotonin syndrome' — The key discriminator: lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia = NMS; clonus + hyperreflexia (especially ankle clonus) = SS. Onset timeline and offending agent class support the differentiation (Boyer and Shannon, N Engl J Med 2005; Strawn et al., Am J Psychiatry 2007).

stem: A 29-year-old woman admitted for a manic episode is started on risperidone. Two days later she is restless, pacing the hallway, unable to sit through meals, and says she 'can't stop moving.' She denies worsening mood symptoms. Which of the following best explains her presentation?
options: A. Worsening mixed mania with motor agitation — increase the risperidone | B. New-onset generalized anxiety disorder unmasked by hospitalization stress | C. Restless legs syndrome — the urge to move is confined to the lower extremities at rest | D. Akathisia — medication-induced inner restlessness from dopamine blockade that worsens with more antipsychotic
answer_text: Akathisia — medication-induced inner restlessness from dopamine blockade that worsens with more antipsychotic
why: Agitation = antipsychotic is the dangerous error: escalating the dopamine blocker intensifies akathisia. Missing the iatrogenic cause leads to a wrong new diagnosis. RLS vs akathisia distinguishes them by distribution and provocation — RLS is limb-specific and rest-provoked; akathisia is global, medication-timed, and worsens with increased dosing.
pearl: Akathisia is the classic inpatient miss — inner restlessness from antipsychotics that worsens with more dopamine blockade, not less.
evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Differential on the unit' — akathisia is the classic miss: restless, driven motor anxiety from antipsychotics that worsens if you reflexively treat it as 'agitation' with more dopamine blockade.

stem: A 28-year-old woman admitted for a severe depressive episode is also found to have untreated PTSD — she endorses daily nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance behaviors that have persisted for two years since an assault. She has no history of substance use disorder. After addressing the acute safety concern, which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for her PTSD?
options: A. Start scheduled lorazepam — benzodiazepines reduce hyperarousal and improve sleep, targeting PTSD's core neurobiological substrate | B. Start an SSRI or SNRI, counsel her about delayed onset, and plan trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) as a discharge goal | C. Start propranolol — beta blockade prevents autonomic consolidation of traumatic memories and is first-line for established PTSD | D. Start an antipsychotic for the intrusive re-experiencing — flashback-like episodes indicate psychotic features requiring dopamine blockade
answer_text: Start an SSRI or SNRI, counsel her about delayed onset, and plan trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) as a discharge goal
why: The reflexive benzodiazepine is the most common trap — standing benzos for PTSD create dependence without treating the disorder and are explicitly avoided on the inpatient unit. SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across all anxiety disorders and PTSD; definitive treatment pairs medication with trauma-focused therapy (prolonged exposure or CPT) planned at discharge. Propranolol is studied in acute peritraumatic settings, not as first-line pharmacotherapy for established PTSD. Antipsychotics conflate re-experiencing with psychosis.
pearl: SSRIs/SNRIs are first-line for PTSD — benzodiazepines are a liability on the unit; pair medication with trauma-focused therapy (PE or CPT) at discharge.
evidence: t_anxiety.md 'Acute inpatient management' — SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD; avoid standing benzodiazepines on the unit; pair pharmacology with disorder-specific behavioral work — prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) for PTSD.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy daily alcohol use is admitted in early withdrawal — tremulous and tachycardic. A nurse is about to start an IV dextrose infusion for a fingerstick glucose in the low-normal range. The most important step before administering the glucose is which of the following?
options: A. Obtain a CIWA-Ar score to guide benzodiazepine dosing before starting any IV fluids | B. Confirm his blood alcohol level has cleared to zero before giving glucose-containing fluids | C. Administer thiamine before or with the glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy | D. Reassure the team that Wernicke encephalopathy risk applies only to patients with a documented prior episode
answer_text: Administer thiamine before or with the glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
why: Sequence error and It's just withdrawal are the traps. Administering carbohydrate to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy — a preventable neurologic emergency. Thiamine goes before or with the glucose, and it does not require a prior history of encephalopathy. The rule governs planned and maintenance carbohydrate, as here: it is not a licence to withhold emergency dextrose from a hypoglycemic patient while thiamine is located.
pearl: Thiamine before or with glucose in a thiamine-depleted patient — carbohydrate loading can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. Never delay emergency dextrose for documented hypoglycemia — give the sugar immediately and the thiamine alongside it.
evidence: t_sud.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Give thiamine before or with glucose; administering carbohydrate to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The sequencing governs maintenance and repletion fluids and never justifies delaying dextrose in documented hypoglycemia.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder is found mute and immobile in her room, staring past the examiner. When the examiner positions her arm in an awkward posture, it remains in place for over a minute. A colleague suggests starting haloperidol for presumed psychosis. Best next step?
options: A. Evaluate for catatonia using a structured rating instrument before initiating any antipsychotic | B. Start haloperidol immediately — mutism and posturing indicate untreated psychosis | C. Apply a physical hold for safety while awaiting psychiatric evaluation | D. Order a urine drug screen and defer further evaluation to the morning team
answer_text: Evaluate for catatonia using a structured rating instrument before initiating any antipsychotic
why: Psychosis = schizophrenia drives the dangerous action: haloperidol in an unexcluded catatonia can precipitate NMS. Waxy flexibility (sustained posturing) is a catatonic sign — catatonia must be rated before any dopamine blocker is started. Restraint first violates least-restrictive principle; Quiet patient = stable patient defers an urgent evaluation.
pearl: Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is excluded — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia; the lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
evidence: catatonia.md 'Management principles' — avoid antipsychotics until catatonia is excluded — they can precipitate or worsen NMS and malignant catatonia. A positive lorazepam challenge both supports the diagnosis and begins treatment.

stem: A 23-year-old man with a history of depression on high-dose sertraline is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after a second serotonergic medication was added to his regimen. Examination shows agitation, diarrhea, diaphoresis, and clonus; reflexes are brisk and symmetrically hyperactive throughout. Temperature is 38.3°C. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
options: A. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — high-dose SSRIs can block dopamine receptors | B. Anticholinergic toxidrome — sertraline has strong anticholinergic activity | C. Alcohol withdrawal — autonomic instability and agitation are hallmarks | D. Serotonin syndrome — rapid onset after a second serotonergic agent was added, with hyperreflexia, clonus, and autonomic instability
answer_text: Serotonin syndrome — rapid onset after a second serotonergic agent was added, with hyperreflexia, clonus, and autonomic instability
why: Wrong toxidrome is the common trap in two directions: NMS (requires a dopamine blocker, slower, lead-pipe rigid) and anticholinergic (dry skin, urinary retention, no clonus). It's just withdrawal misreads autonomic instability without the serotonin-specific signs. Serotonin syndrome is the answer: rapid onset after serotonergic augmentation, clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability are its distinguishing features.
pearl: Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia after a serotonergic agent was added. NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK, on a dopamine blocker — slower and stiffer.
evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, and autonomic instability with rapid onset, usually after a serotonergic agent was started or increased. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: 'lead-pipe' rigidity, hyperthermia, and elevated CK in someone on a dopamine blocker — slower and stiffer than serotonin syndrome.

stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has just been started on clozapine. He reports feeling better than he has in years. The treatment team asks the student to identify the most critical ongoing monitoring parameter for this medication. Which of the following is correct?
options: A. Monthly liver function tests — clozapine is heavily metabolized by the liver and hepatotoxicity is the primary dose-limiting toxicity | B. Absolute neutrophil count monitoring per prescribing requirements — clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis | C. Serum clozapine levels at every visit — toxicity is reliably predicted by drug concentration | D. Monthly QTc interval on ECG — clozapine's primary dose-limiting toxicity is cardiac arrhythmia
answer_text: Absolute neutrophil count monitoring per prescribing requirements — clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis
why: Wrong monitoring target in two forms — LFTs and QTc — and Treat the number not the patient (serum levels without ANC) are the traps. Clozapine's mandated monitoring is the absolute neutrophil count due to the risk of potentially fatal agranulocytosis. Serum levels and LFTs may be checked but do not constitute the primary safety obligation.
pearl: Clozapine requires mandatory ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis; also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.
evidence: psychopharm_primer.md — Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia: ANC monitoring per prescribing information; also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation/ileus, and seizures.

stem: A 19-year-old man is admitted after a near-lethal suicide attempt. He has expressed persistent hopelessness and a stated wish to die for three days. On hospital day 4, nurses report he seems 'much better' — calm, well-rested, and telling the team he is ready to go home. His affect is bright and he is chatty with staff. No clinical change or social development explains the shift. Best next step?
options: A. Begin discharge planning — improvement is the goal of admission and this patient has achieved it | B. Reduce his observation level and move him to a lower-acuity room to reinforce the progress | C. Escalate to the attending immediately — unexplained sudden improvement after severe suicidality is a warning sign requiring reassessment | D. Update the safety plan and schedule discharge within 24 hours while the patient is engaged
answer_text: Escalate to the attending immediately — unexplained sudden improvement after severe suicidality is a warning sign requiring reassessment
why: Sudden improvement = recovery is the most dangerous trap: the pocket card explicitly lists unexplained sudden improvement as an immediate escalation trigger. Quiet patient = stable patient reduces vigilance at exactly the wrong moment. Safety plan = discharge permission slip conflates a tool with a risk decision.
pearl: Sudden unexplained improvement after severe suicidality is an escalation trigger, not evidence of recovery.
evidence: pg_suicide.md 'What to escalate immediately' — Sudden improvement after severe suicidality without clear explanation.

stem: A patient is pacing the hallway, speaking loudly, and waving his hands. He has not threatened anyone and is not in immediate danger of harming himself or others. You are the student. Which response is best?
options: A. Let a nearby staff member know you are engaging, then approach calmly — without blocking his exit or yours — introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter where staff can still see us, or is there something I can get you?' | B. Return to the nursing station and request a PRN intramuscular medication order before approaching | C. Call for additional staff and prepare for restraint in case the patient escalates | D. Instruct him firmly to return to his room or staff will have to intervene
answer_text: Let a nearby staff member know you are engaging, then approach calmly — without blocking his exit or yours — introduce yourself, acknowledge that he looks upset, and offer him a choice — 'Would it help to step somewhere quieter where staff can still see us, or is there something I can get you?'
why: Agitation = antipsychotic, Restraint first, and Commands over choices are the three forms of the same error: defaulting to force or medication before de-escalation. The Project BETA framework begins with calm presence, acknowledgment of distress, and genuine choices — not commands or preemptive escalation.
pearl: Verbal de-escalation — calm presence, acknowledgment, and genuine choices — is the default first response to agitation, not a courtesy step before medication; tell a staff member before you engage, and stay near your exit without blocking the patient's.
evidence: agitation.md 'Verbal de-escalation, first' — This is the default response, not a courtesy step. The Project BETA de-escalation framework (Richmond et al. 2012) centers respect, simple boundaries, listening, and offering choices rather than issuing commands.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder tells her student doctor that she trusts only her and that the other staff 'just don't care.' Night nurses describe her as cooperative and warm; day nurses report she screams at them. How is this pattern best understood?
options: A. The patient has genuine rapport with the student and a legitimate complaint about day staff behavior | B. Splitting — a feature of BPD in which people are experienced as entirely good or bad, requiring team consistency as the antidote | C. Deliberate manipulation — the patient is consciously exploiting the split to get preferential treatment | D. A delusional belief about staff intentions that warrants diagnostic reassessment for a psychotic disorder
answer_text: Splitting — a feature of BPD in which people are experienced as entirely good or bad, requiring team consistency as the antidote
why: Face-value reassurance takes the report at face value and misses the clinical process. Manipulation framing leads to punitive responses that worsen therapeutic alliance. Psychosis = schizophrenia misapplies a diagnostic frame to a personality-disorder phenomenon. Splitting — all-good or all-bad experiencing of staff — is a feature of BPD; the intervention is team communication and consistency, not confrontation.
pearl: Splitting is a feature of BPD, not a character flaw — team consistency and shared notes are the antidote, not confrontation.
evidence: t_personality.md — Splitting — experiencing staff as all-good or all-bad — is common and is a feature of the illness, not a character flaw or manipulation.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted in crisis with severe anxiety and sleep disturbance. She has been engaged in DBT for six months with good skill use documented. She is asking for 'something for her nerves.' The pharmacologic approach most consistent with evidence-based practice for BPD is which of the following?
options: A. Prescribe lorazepam PRN — addressing the anxiety will help her engage with skills | B. Add a nightly benzodiazepine for sleep — insomnia is fueling the crisis cycle | C. Add an SSRI — anxiety in a BPD patient with good DBT engagement suggests an undertreated mood component requiring pharmacological augmentation. | D. Minimize pharmacotherapy — if needed, a single low-risk agent for ≤1 week, preferring a sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine over a benzodiazepine.
answer_text: Minimize pharmacotherapy — if needed, a single low-risk agent for ≤1 week, preferring a sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine over a benzodiazepine.
why: The reflexive benzodiazepine in two forms (PRN and scheduled) and Polypharmacy first are the traps. No medication treats BPD itself; the evidence base supports skills over pills, and benzodiazepines in BPD carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023). The NICE-aligned approach is a single, low-risk agent at the minimum dose for ≤1 week — sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine preferred over benzodiazepines.
pearl: Benzodiazepines in BPD carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any class studied — reach for skills, not pills.
evidence: t_personality.md — do not start or escalate benzodiazepines — they carry the highest risk of attempted or completed suicide of any psychotropic class studied in BPD (HR 1.61, Lieslehto 2023) and worsen disinhibition. If a crisis genuinely needs pharmacology, follow the NICE rule: a single agent at the minimum effective dose for ≤1 week (prefer a sedating antihistamine or low-dose quetiapine over benzodiazepines and TCAs).

stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the inpatient unit by his parents after three weeks of dramatically decreased need for sleep (sleeping two to three hours and feeling rested), expansive and grandiose mood, pressured speech, and impulsive spending. His parents note he has always been 'a little hyper' in school but never like this. He takes no medications and denies substance use. Most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Bipolar disorder, manic episode — the episodic 3-week course with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity distinguishes this from ADHD | B. ADHD, first recognized in adulthood — the impulsivity and hyperactivity confirm childhood-onset ADHD now decompensated | C. Brief psychotic disorder — the grandiosity indicates loss of reality testing | D. Adjustment disorder — the academic stress of college explains the sleep changes and mood elevation
answer_text: Bipolar disorder, manic episode — the episodic 3-week course with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity distinguishes this from ADHD
why: ADHD vs mania is the key discrimination: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood, not episodic with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity. Psychosis = schizophrenia misreads a mood symptom as a primary psychotic feature. Adjustment by default collapses a manic episode into a stress reaction.
pearl: ADHD is chronic and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic — episodic ADHD-like symptoms are a mood or substance flag.
evidence: t_neurodev.md — ADHD vs bipolar mania: ADHD is chronic, pervasive, and cross-situational from childhood; mania is episodic with mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity. Episodic 'ADHD-like' symptoms are a mood or substance flag.

stem: An autistic adult admitted after aggression at his group home is increasingly distressed on the inpatient unit — covering his ears, rocking, and repeatedly asking when it will be quiet. He is not in imminent danger. No PRN medication has been given. The most appropriate first step is which of the following?
options: A. Administer a PRN antipsychotic — irritability and agitation in autism respond to targeted medication | B. Engage him in a group activity to normalize the milieu and reduce his isolation | C. Move him to a quieter space and establish a predictable routine to reduce sensory load | D. Assign a staff member to redirect him verbally and prompt use of calming strategies
answer_text: Move him to a quieter space and establish a predictable routine to reduce sensory load
why: Agitation = antipsychotic skips the evidence-based first step. Group = stimulation adds sensory load when reduction is the goal. Verbal prompting first increases auditory demand on an already overloaded sensory system. The environment-first approach — quiet space, predictable routine, reduced sensory input — is the foundational intervention in ASD on the inpatient unit.
pearl: In ASD, lead with the environment — predictability, reduced sensory load, and concrete communication — before reaching for medication.
evidence: t_neurodev.md — Lead with the environment and communication, not medication. Provide predictability (routine, visual schedules, consistent staff), reduce sensory load, allow extra processing time, use concrete language.

stem: A 16-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa has been restrictive for 4 months and is medically admitted with critically low weight. Before nutritional rehabilitation begins, which approach most directly reduces the risk of refeeding syndrome?
options: A. Start full nutritional rehabilitation immediately at a standard adult caloric target to restore weight as rapidly as possible. | B. Give prophylactic anxiolytics and monitor for 24 hours before introducing nutrition — anxiety increases metabolic demand in malnourished patients. | C. Correct all electrolyte abnormalities to normal before introducing any nutrition — electrolyte imbalances worsen if nutrition begins before they are stable. | D. Start caloric refeeding at a conservative initial target and advance slowly; administer thiamine before or with carbohydrate and check phosphate, potassium, and magnesium at least daily early in refeeding.
answer_text: Start caloric refeeding at a conservative initial target and advance slowly; administer thiamine before or with carbohydrate and check phosphate, potassium, and magnesium at least daily early in refeeding.
why: Faster is safer, Sedation before nutrition, and Normalize first all create delay or metabolic risk. The source's 'start low, go slow' principle is the safety framework: conservative start, daily electrolyte checks, and thiamine before carbohydrate to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
pearl: Refeeding syndrome prevention: start low, go slow, give thiamine before carbohydrate, check phosphate daily.
evidence: t_eating.md — Refeeding syndrome: the safe posture is 'start low, go slow': begin conservative caloric refeeding, check phosphate/potassium/magnesium at least daily early, supplement phosphate and give thiamine before or with carbohydrate, and advance calories per protocol as electrolytes stay stable.

stem: A 27-year-old mother, 9 days postpartum, arrives with acute confusion and delusions that her infant 'was sent to test her faith.' Her husband reports hours of apparent lucidity followed by rapid deterioration. The diagnosis of postpartum psychosis is made. Which management priority is most immediately critical?
options: A. Refer for outpatient psychiatry follow-up and prescribe a low-dose antipsychotic — postpartum psychosis in first-time mothers without prior mental illness typically resolves with minimal intervention. | B. Immediate psychiatric hospitalization — postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency; explicitly assess and restrict unsupervised access to the infant, start acute pharmacotherapy (lithium or antipsychotic), and protect sleep. | C. Prioritize medical workup to rule out thyroid dysfunction and eclampsia before any psychiatric treatment — pharmacotherapy is premature until medical causes are excluded. | D. The lucid interval between episodes provides reassurance — waxing-and-waning symptoms are inconsistent with psychosis; this is most likely a severe postpartum adjustment reaction.
answer_text: Immediate psychiatric hospitalization — postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency; explicitly assess and restrict unsupervised access to the infant, start acute pharmacotherapy (lithium or antipsychotic), and protect sleep.
why: Outpatient sufficient and Lucid interval = reassurance miss the emergency framing. Medical workup before treatment is wrong only in its sequencing: delirium, eclampsia, thyroid disease, infection, and autoimmune encephalitis are excluded concurrently with emergency psychiatric admission — the organic workup proceeds in parallel and must never delay hospitalization or treatment. The source states: 'POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently.' The safety assessment must explicitly include the infant.
pearl: Postpartum psychosis = immediate hospitalization, restrict unsupervised infant access, start lithium or antipsychotic urgently.
evidence: t_perinatal.md — POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS IS A PSYCHIATRIC EMERGENCY: rapid onset, waxing/waning presentation, and real risk to both mother and infant — admit and treat urgently. The safety assessment must explicitly include the infant: assess risk to the baby, the parent's current access to the baby, and available supervision.

stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia is voluntarily admitted and refuses his prescribed antipsychotic. When asked, he explains what the medication is for, articulates specific concerns about its side effects, understands the risks of not taking it, and asks whether alternatives exist. Best next step?
options: A. Conduct a formal capacity assessment; if he has capacity, his refusal must be respected, documented, and an alternative offered | B. Override the refusal — voluntarily admitted patients accept the prescribed treatment plan as a condition of admission | C. Seek an emergency court order — a schizophrenia diagnosis with medication refusal requires judicial review | D. Discharge him against medical advice — he is voluntary and refusing treatment
answer_text: Conduct a formal capacity assessment; if he has capacity, his refusal must be respected, documented, and an alternative offered
why: Refusal = no capacity in two forms — assumed from admission type and assumed from diagnosis — is the central error. Capacity is decision-specific and clinical: the four abilities are assessed, not inferred from the admission voluntary/involuntary status or from a psychiatric diagnosis. Discharge for refusal conflates refusal with grounds for discharge. This patient's demonstrated abilities (communicating, understanding, appreciating, reasoning) point toward capacity — in which case his refusal must be honored.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and clinical — a psychiatric diagnosis and even a refusal do not equal incapacity; assess the four abilities.
evidence: ethics_legal.md — Capacity is decision-specific and clinical (a physician assesses it). The four abilities: communicate a choice, understand, appreciate, and reason. Competent patients (including many involuntarily hospitalized ones) generally retain the right to refuse medication. Overriding that refusal requires either a true emergency or a separate legal/adjudicated process.

stem: An outpatient therapist is meeting with a 34-year-old patient who describes, in specific detail, a plan to assault a named family member. He states his intent to act before the end of the week and describes the location and means. The therapist's obligation is which of the following?
options: A. Maintain confidentiality — disclosing the patient's statements would violate the therapeutic relationship and deter future help-seeking | B. Document the threat and continue outpatient treatment with increased session frequency | C. Take reasonable protective steps — which may include warning the potential victim, notifying law enforcement, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment | D. Wait for corroborating evidence before acting — a single session disclosure does not establish genuine intent
answer_text: Take reasonable protective steps — which may include warning the potential victim, notifying law enforcement, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment
why: Confidentiality always wins, Document and continue, and Wait for action are three forms of inaction in the face of the duty to protect. A specific, credible threat to a named, identifiable person — with described means and timeline — triggers a duty to take reasonable protective steps. The options are broad: warning the victim, notifying police, hospitalizing, or intensifying treatment. The duty does not require certainty that harm will occur.
pearl: A specific, credible threat to a reasonably identifiable victim overrides confidentiality — the duty to protect obligates action, not only documentation.
evidence: ethics_legal.md — When a patient makes a serious threat of violence against a reasonably identifiable victim, the clinician has a duty to take reasonable protective steps — which may include warning the potential victim, notifying police, hospitalizing the patient, or intensifying treatment.

stem: A family meeting is held on hospital day 3 for a 29-year-old man admitted for a first manic episode. His mother interrupts repeatedly: 'He does this every time he stops his medication — he's selfish and he makes us all suffer.' She is tearful and wringing her hands. The attending invites the student to observe what is happening. What is the student's best understanding of this dynamic?
options: A. The mother's criticism is accurate and should be incorporated into the discharge plan as a documented adherence barrier | B. The meeting should be suspended — the mother's distress is dysregulating the patient and the therapeutic goals cannot be met | C. The mother should be gently corrected about the medication-stopping narrative to address the factual inaccuracy | D. The mother is showing expressed emotion — criticism that likely masks fear and grief — and the student's task is to validate the feeling behind it before moving to problem-solving
answer_text: The mother is showing expressed emotion — criticism that likely masks fear and grief — and the student's task is to validate the feeling behind it before moving to problem-solving
why: Criticism as fact accepts EE as objective reporting; Terminate for emotion cuts off the highest-yield phase of the meeting; Correct the narrative redirects to facts before the emotional climate has been heard. Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — is the measurable family dynamic that predicts relapse. De-shaming and validating the underlying fear or grief, without correcting in the moment, is what the playbook calls the phase that most changes outcomes.
pearl: Expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement — often masks fear; validate it without correcting it in the moment, because this phase is where outcomes change.
evidence: family_playbook.md 'Hear the family and read the emotional climate' — Listen for expressed emotion — criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement — without correcting it in the moment. De-shame: frame symptoms and behavior as illness and regulation, not character or fault. This is the phase that most changes outcomes; protect the time for it.

stem: An 82-year-old man on postoperative day 2 after hip arthroplasty is confused and agitated. The Confusion Assessment Method is positive for delirium. He has no history of dementia. Which is the most appropriate initial management step?
options: A. Start scheduled haloperidol — antipsychotics prevent delirium progression in post-surgical patients. | B. Implement non-pharmacologic delirium measures — reorientation, sleep-wake protection, early mobilization, sensory restoration — investigate the underlying cause, and deprescribe deliriogenic medications. | C. Start a benzodiazepine PRN — GABAergic agents calm delirium-related agitation while the cause is sought. | D. Order a STAT non-contrast CT head — new confusion in a post-surgical patient indicates intracranial pathology until proven otherwise.
answer_text: Implement non-pharmacologic delirium measures — reorientation, sleep-wake protection, early mobilization, sensory restoration — investigate the underlying cause, and deprescribe deliriogenic medications.
why: Agitation = antipsychotic is the most dangerous trap — scheduled antipsychotics are not for delirium prevention and carry a mortality warning in older patients with dementia-related psychosis. The reflexive benzodiazepine deepens delirium unless the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal. Non-pharmacologic measures — reorientation, sleep-wake cycle protection, early mobilization, sensory aids, deprescribing — are first-line while the cause is found.
pearl: Non-pharmacologic measures (ABCDEF bundle, sensory aids, mobility) are first-line for delirium — antipsychotics are for dangerous agitation only, never for prevention.
evidence: delirium.md 'Management' — Non-pharmacologic measures come first, not as an afterthought: reorient the patient, protect the sleep–wake cycle, mobilize early, restore sensory aids. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation only — not for prevention.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease is admitted from her nursing home after 2 days of worsening confusion. A CAM is positive. She is agitated and picking at her IV. The team asks the student to help select an appropriate PRN medication for dangerous agitation. Which of the following is correct?
options: A. A benzodiazepine is the safest first choice — GABAergic agents are better tolerated than antipsychotics in cognitively impaired older patients. | B. Start a scheduled antipsychotic to prevent further deterioration — treating the agitation reduces downstream complications. | C. Combine a benzodiazepine with a low-dose antipsychotic for the best coverage of mixed delirium-related agitation. | D. If pharmacotherapy is needed after non-pharmacologic measures fail, use the lowest effective antipsychotic dose time-limited with close monitoring; avoid benzodiazepines unless the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
answer_text: If pharmacotherapy is needed after non-pharmacologic measures fail, use the lowest effective antipsychotic dose time-limited with close monitoring; avoid benzodiazepines unless the cause is alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
why: The reflexive benzodiazepine and Agitation = antipsychotic are both active. Benzodiazepines are appropriate only for alcohol and sedative withdrawal — in other delirium they worsen confusion and increase aspiration and fall risk. If pharmacotherapy is needed for dangerous agitation after non-pharmacologic measures, a low-dose antipsychotic time-limited is the choice. Polypharmacy before non-pharmacologic management is never the correct framework.
pearl: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium — reserve them for alcohol and sedative withdrawal only; antipsychotics at the lowest effective dose, time-limited, for dangerous agitation.
evidence: delirium.md 'Management' — Avoid benzodiazepines, with the single exception of alcohol or sedative withdrawal, where they are the treatment. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation only — lowest effective dose, time-limited.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of vivid recurrent visual hallucinations (small animals in the room), episodes of staring with fluctuating cognition, mild rigidity and slowness, and his wife's report that he 'acts out his dreams' and has struck her while asleep. Which dementia subtype does this constellation most strongly suggest?
options: A. Lewy body dementia — the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder is the characteristic core-feature tetrad. | B. Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — visual hallucinations and behavioral change point to frontotemporal degeneration. | C. Alzheimer disease — amnestic dementia with behavioral symptoms in a 74-year-old is most commonly Alzheimer. | D. Vascular dementia — stepwise decline with parkinsonism and motor slowing points to cerebrovascular disease.
answer_text: Lewy body dementia — the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder is the characteristic core-feature tetrad.
why: Most common = correct drives most errors here: Alzheimer is most prevalent, but the full LBD tetrad — fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder — is present. FTD shows disinhibition and personality change without this constellation. Vascular dementia follows a stepwise course with focal signs, not this tetrad. Recognizing LBD matters urgently because of its neuroleptic sensitivity.
pearl: LBD tetrad: fluctuating cognition + recurrent visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behavior disorder — recognize it before anyone prescribes an antipsychotic.
evidence: t_neurocog.md — Lewy body dementia — fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, REM sleep behavior disorder, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity.

stem: A patient with known Lewy body dementia is admitted with agitation and paranoid delusions. A nurse asks whether the team should start haloperidol. The most appropriate response is which of the following?
options: A. Start haloperidol — first-generation antipsychotics are better tolerated in elderly patients than second-generation agents. | B. Start olanzapine — second-generation antipsychotics do not carry neuroleptic sensitivity risk in LBD. | C. Hold the antipsychotic, flag the LBD diagnosis to the team, pursue non-pharmacologic management first, and reserve quetiapine or pimavanserin if pharmacotherapy is truly unavoidable. | D. Start risperidone — its lower EPS profile compared to haloperidol makes it the safest antipsychotic for LBD.
answer_text: Hold the antipsychotic, flag the LBD diagnosis to the team, pursue non-pharmacologic management first, and reserve quetiapine or pimavanserin if pharmacotherapy is truly unavoidable.
why: Newer = better in three forms. In LBD, neuroleptic sensitivity can be triggered by any dopamine-blocking agent — the risk is highest with typicals and substantial with high-D2-occupancy SGAs like risperidone and olanzapine. The correct first step is flagging the diagnosis, non-pharmacologic management, and choosing quetiapine or pimavanserin if medication is truly unavoidable.
pearl: Avoid antipsychotics in LBD — especially typicals; if pharmacotherapy is unavoidable, quetiapine or pimavanserin are lower-risk choices.
evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — In Lewy body dementia, avoid antipsychotics (especially typicals) because of life-threatening neuroleptic sensitivity — if one is unavoidable, quetiapine or pimavanserin are lower-risk choices.

stem: A 69-year-old man is referred for evaluation of progressive cognitive decline, urinary incontinence that preceded the cognitive changes by several months, and a gait his wife describes as 'shuffling and magnetic — like his feet are stuck to the floor.' MRI is pending. Which diagnosis should be considered first because of its potential reversibility?
options: A. Alzheimer disease — amnestic-predominant decline with gait changes in a 69-year-old is most likely AD. | B. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus — the triad of magnetic gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence is potentially reversible with ventriculoperitoneal shunting. | C. Vascular dementia — gait dysfunction and cognitive decline indicate stepwise cerebrovascular disease. | D. Parkinson disease dementia — gait dysfunction and cognitive decline indicate a Lewy body spectrum disorder.
answer_text: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus — the triad of magnetic gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence is potentially reversible with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
why: Most common = correct drives most errors. The specific triad — wet (urinary incontinence), wacky (cognitive decline), and wobbly (magnetic gait) — is classic NPH, and its potential reversibility with shunting makes it a must-diagnose. The magnetic gait is low-clearance, wide-based, and apraxic — different from Parkinsonian tremor-and-rigidity gait. Early incontinence preceding cognition is unusual for Alzheimer or vascular dementia at this stage.
pearl: NPH triad = wet, wacky, wobbly (urinary incontinence, cognition, magnetic gait) — potentially reversible with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
evidence: t_neurocog.md — normal-pressure hydrocephalus (the triad — wet, wacky, wobbly: urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, magnetic gait).

stem: Psychiatry is consulted on an 82-year-old man in the surgical ICU on postoperative day 3. He is quiet, slow to respond, and sleeping between nursing checks — his nurse reports he was interactive at yesterday's evening assessment. His CAM is positive. The covering team wonders why this presentation is more concerning than a 'hyperactive' delirious patient. Which statement best explains the clinical risk?
options: A. Hyperactive delirium carries worse outcomes — the agitation, pulling at lines, and fall risk create more immediate danger than a quiet, withdrawn presentation. | B. The two subtypes have equivalent outcomes — motor presentation does not predict prognosis; treatment targets the underlying cause regardless of subtype. | C. Hypoactive delirium responds better to antipsychotics — the reduced agitation creates a therapeutic window for pharmacologic intervention that hyperactive delirium does not allow. | D. Hypoactive delirium carries worse outcomes precisely because it goes unrecognized — the quiet, non-interactive patient does not trigger intervention; it is commonly mislabeled as depression and associated with higher mortality.
answer_text: Hypoactive delirium carries worse outcomes precisely because it goes unrecognized — the quiet, non-interactive patient does not trigger intervention; it is commonly mislabeled as depression and associated with higher mortality.
why: Hyperactive = higher risk, Subtypes equivalent, and Hypoactive = better pharmacologic target all invert the clinical reality. The source states: 'The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient.' Recognition requires deliberate screening — the CAM is the tool.
pearl: Hypoactive delirium = the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, easily mislabeled as depression.
evidence: delirium.md — The hypoactive form is the one that gets missed, and it carries worse outcomes precisely because no one is alarmed by a quiet patient. Hypoactive delirium is the dangerous one: commonly missed, worse outcomes, and easily mislabeled as depression.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is admitted after 4 months of progressive cognitive decline and withdrawal. Neuropsychological testing suggests a moderate amnestic syndrome. She has no known prior psychiatric or neurological history. Which is the most appropriate first-line laboratory workup before assigning a neurodegenerative diagnosis?
options: A. CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and consider RPR/HIV — reversible causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis is established. | B. Anti-NMDA receptor antibody panel — autoimmune encephalitis mimics dementia and should be ruled out first in all new presentations. | C. Brain MRI with gadolinium — structural imaging is the single most important diagnostic step for a new dementia presentation. | D. APOE genotyping — an APOE ε4 allele would confirm Alzheimer disease and guide management.
answer_text: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and consider RPR/HIV — reversible causes must be excluded before a neurodegenerative diagnosis is established.
why: Jump to autoimmune and Genetic confirmation both skip the foundational step. The reversible-cause panel — B12/folate, TSH, CMP, and when indicated RPR/HIV — must precede neurodegenerative labeling because these conditions are treatable and clinically indistinguishable at presentation. APOE genotyping is not a diagnostic standard. Structural imaging is part of the same initial workup rather than a later step, but it is not the laboratory screen this stem asks for, and it does not require gadolinium.
pearl: Every new cognitive diagnosis gets both halves of the reversible screen: the panel (B12/folate, TSH, CMP, ± RPR/HIV) and structural imaging — labs cannot exclude NPH or a chronic subdural.
evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Initial workup' — Labs to catch reversible causes: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12/folate, and — when indicated — HIV and RPR/treponemal testing. Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) as part of the initial workup of any new cognitive diagnosis — it is the only way the NPH and chronic subdural hematoma on the reversible list above get found — with MRI preferred, and expedited for atypical, rapid, focal, or early-onset presentations.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment is admitted for worsening confusion and agitation over the past week. She recently started diphenhydramine nightly for insomnia and oxybutynin for urge incontinence. The student reviews her medication list. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Add risperidone for the agitation — it is the most evidence-based pharmacotherapy for behavioral symptoms in cognitive impairment. | B. Order a 24-hour EEG — medication-induced encephalopathy can produce seizure patterns that explain cognitive worsening. | C. Flag diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as high-risk anticholinergic agents for the team, escalate for deprescribing, and recommend non-pharmacologic sleep and bladder strategies. | D. Reassure the family that mild cognitive impairment commonly worsens under medical stress and will recover once she is discharged.
answer_text: Flag diphenhydramine and oxybutynin as high-risk anticholinergic agents for the team, escalate for deprescribing, and recommend non-pharmacologic sleep and bladder strategies.
why: Agitation = antipsychotic and Face-value reassurance both bypass the diagnosis. Anticholinergic burden is a recognized, reversible driver of cognitive worsening in older adults — diphenhydramine and oxybutynin are among the Beers Criteria's most flagged agents. Jump to testing substitutes cost for the straightforward clinical action. The geriatric psychiatry principle: the drug list is often the diagnosis; deprescribing is active treatment.
pearl: In older adults with cognitive change, the medication list is often the diagnosis — assess anticholinergic burden and deprescribe before adding anything.
evidence: t_geri.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Apply the Beers Criteria and assess cumulative anticholinergic burden, then actively deprescribe deliriogenic and high-risk agents. 'High-yield pearls' — The drug list is often the diagnosis — deprescribing is active treatment.

stem: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who reports an 18-month history of increasingly disinhibited behavior — making inappropriate sexual comments to strangers, hoarding food, and neglecting hygiene. He has no memory complaints, names and recognizes objects normally, and denies mood symptoms. Neuropsychological testing shows prominent executive dysfunction with intact episodic memory. Most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Bipolar disorder — new-onset mania presents with disinhibition, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction in midlife. | B. Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — early disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior, and executive dysfunction with relative sparing of episodic memory in a younger adult is the classic bvFTD presentation. | C. Early-onset Alzheimer disease — insidious behavioral change in a 58-year-old is most commonly early-onset AD. | D. Personality disorder — disinhibition, impulsivity, and boundary violations reflect a longstanding personality pattern rather than a new neurological process.
answer_text: Behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia — early disinhibition, socially inappropriate behavior, and executive dysfunction with relative sparing of episodic memory in a younger adult is the classic bvFTD presentation.
why: Bipolar by default, Most common = correct, and Personality disorder by default are three forms of the same error: assigning a functional psychiatric diagnosis before considering neurodegeneration. FTD is the dementia of younger adults, presenting with behavior and personality change or progressive language, while sparing episodic memory early — the exact opposite of Alzheimer.
pearl: Frontotemporal dementia: younger onset, behavioral disinhibition or progressive language first, episodic memory spared early — the signature that separates it from Alzheimer.
evidence: t_neurocog.md — Frontotemporal — younger onset with early personality/behavior change or progressive aphasia; memory relatively spared early.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. She has developed, over the past month, a fixed belief that her neighbors are poisoning her food and has stopped eating. She is alert, coherent, and oriented. There is no mood disturbance. Which is the most important next step?
options: A. Diagnose late-onset schizophrenia — paranoid delusions in late life unexplained by a mood disorder represent a primary psychotic illness. | B. Start an antipsychotic immediately — the refusal to eat constitutes an acute safety emergency requiring empirical treatment. | C. Reassure the family that paranoid ideation is a normal variant of cognitive aging. | D. Conduct a medical workup to exclude organic causes of new-onset psychosis — including delirium, medication effect, CNS lesion, metabolic derangement, and autoimmune encephalitis — before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis.
answer_text: Conduct a medical workup to exclude organic causes of new-onset psychosis — including delirium, medication effect, CNS lesion, metabolic derangement, and autoimmune encephalitis — before establishing a primary psychiatric diagnosis.
why: Psychosis = schizophrenia, Treat before diagnosis, and Face-value reassurance all skip the foundational step. New-onset psychosis in an older adult without a prior psychiatric history is a medical emergency until proven otherwise. The differential includes delirium, CNS lesion, metabolic cause, autoimmune encephalitis, and medication-induced psychosis — all requiring workup before a primary psychotic diagnosis is made.
pearl: New psychosis in an older adult is a medical emergency until proven otherwise — work up before labeling or treating.
evidence: t_geri.md 'High-yield pearls' — New psychosis in an older adult is delirium or a medical cause until proven otherwise.

stem: A 35-year-old man with bipolar disorder screens positive for catatonia on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale — he is mute, maintains awkward arm postures for extended periods, and stares past the examiner. The team has appropriately held the antipsychotic. What is the indicated next step?
options: A. Administer a lorazepam challenge (IV or IM) — meaningful improvement in catatonic signs after benzodiazepines supports the diagnosis and begins treatment; benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia. | B. Initiate a clozapine trial — persistent psychiatric symptoms after stopping the antipsychotic indicate a need for a clozapine evaluation. | C. Restart the antipsychotic at a lower dose — catatonic symptoms worsen without dopamine blockade and the patient needs partial antipsychotic coverage. | D. Apply soft restraints and obtain an urgent head CT to rule out structural causes before proceeding with any treatment.
answer_text: Administer a lorazepam challenge (IV or IM) — meaningful improvement in catatonic signs after benzodiazepines supports the diagnosis and begins treatment; benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia.
why: Clozapine for catatonia, Restart antipsychotic, and Restraint before treatment all defer or undermine first-line treatment. The catatonia source states: 'A test dose of lorazepam is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment — a meaningful, often rapid improvement supports the diagnosis and predicts response.' Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.
pearl: After positive catatonia screen + holding the antipsychotic → lorazepam challenge next: both diagnostic and therapeutic.
evidence: catatonia.md 'The lorazepam challenge' — A test dose of lorazepam (IV or IM) is both a diagnostic maneuver and the start of treatment; meaningful improvement after the challenge supports the diagnosis and predicts benzodiazepine response. Benzodiazepines are first-line; ECT is for benzodiazepine-refractory or malignant catatonia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been mute and posturing for 2 days. Today she is found febrile to 39.6°C, diaphoretic, hypotensive, with lead-pipe rigidity and a markedly elevated CK. Her antipsychotic was increased yesterday. Best next step?
options: A. Administer additional lorazepam challenge doses and observe on the psychiatric unit — the rigidity suggests catatonic stupor responding to benzodiazepines. | B. Increase the antipsychotic — this is a catatonic variant of treatment-resistant psychosis requiring more aggressive dopamine blockade. | C. Stop all antipsychotics immediately, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring and supportive care, and obtain urgent psychiatric and neurology consultation — ECT should be considered for malignant or refractory catatonia. | D. Treat empirically for sepsis — fever, hypotension, and elevated CK indicate bacterial infection requiring antibiotics.
answer_text: Stop all antipsychotics immediately, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring and supportive care, and obtain urgent psychiatric and neurology consultation — ECT should be considered for malignant or refractory catatonia.
why: Underestimate the emergency and Agitation = antipsychotic are the two clinical catastrophes. This is NMS/malignant catatonia: fever, autonomic instability, lead-pipe rigidity, elevated CK after antipsychotic escalation. The correct sequence is stop all antipsychotics, transfer to a medical unit for hemodynamic monitoring, continue lorazepam — benzodiazepines remain first-line pharmacotherapy for malignant catatonia while ECT is arranged — and pursue ECT emergently if the patient does not rapidly improve; the error in option A is observation on the psychiatric unit, not the lorazepam, and certainly not more antipsychotic.
pearl: Malignant catatonia overlaps with NMS: fever + rigidity + elevated CK + autonomic instability after antipsychotic exposure — stop antipsychotics, transfer to medical, and consider ECT urgently.
evidence: catatonia.md — The emergency you must never miss is malignant catatonia: autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and rigidity that clinically overlaps with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). ECT is the treatment for severe, malignant, or benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia and should not be delayed when the patient is deteriorating.

stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease is currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. His neurologist asks the student to identify what pharmacotherapy optimization is supported by evidence for this stage of disease.
options: A. Increase donepezil to the maximum tolerated dose — dose escalation of cholinesterase inhibitors alone is the evidence-based approach for moderate-to-severe disease. | B. Add memantine — combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine (NMDA antagonist) is the evidence-based pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease. | C. Switch to a rivastigmine patch — transdermal delivery is more effective than oral donepezil in advanced disease. | D. Start a monoclonal anti-amyloid antibody — these agents are now standard of care for all stages of Alzheimer.
answer_text: Add memantine — combination of a cholinesterase inhibitor and memantine (NMDA antagonist) is the evidence-based pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.
why: Dose escalation alone and Newer = better in two forms. For mild-to-moderate AD, cholinesterase inhibitors alone are the standard. For moderate-to-severe AD, adding memantine is the evidence-based optimization. Anti-amyloid antibodies are specialist-initiated, amyloid-confirmed, and restricted to early disease.
pearl: Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild-to-moderate AD; add memantine for moderate-to-severe disease.
evidence: t_neurocog.md 'Acute inpatient management' — Cognitive symptoms: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild–moderate Alzheimer/Lewy body disease; add memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate–severe disease.

stem: A 73-year-old woman with recurrent major depression (last treated 5 years ago) is referred for cognitive evaluation after 3 months of 'memory problems.' On formal cognitive testing she scores in the impaired range on delayed recall but consistently answers 'I don't know' rather than confabulating; she is slow to initiate answers and appears effortfully disengaged. She remains alert and attentive, and scores 22 on the PHQ-9. Most appropriate next step?
options: A. Diagnose major neurocognitive disorder — the cognitive test scores confirm a dementia syndrome independent of mood. | B. Start a cholinesterase inhibitor — the episodic memory impairment indicates Alzheimer-spectrum disease requiring pharmacotherapy. | C. Order an amyloid PET scan — direct amyloid visualization definitively distinguishes depression-associated cognitive impairment from Alzheimer disease. | D. Prioritize treatment of the depressive episode and reassess cognitive function after remission — the pattern of 'I don't know' responses, effortful disengagement, and a PHQ-9 of 22 is consistent with pseudodementia that may resolve with antidepressant treatment.
answer_text: Prioritize treatment of the depressive episode and reassess cognitive function after remission — the pattern of 'I don't know' responses, effortful disengagement, and a PHQ-9 of 22 is consistent with pseudodementia that may resolve with antidepressant treatment.
why: Scores = diagnosis, Treat the number not the patient, and Jump to advanced imaging all bypass the pseudodementia maneuver. 'I don't know' responses with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — rather than confabulation and unawareness — is the clinical signature of depression-associated cognitive impairment (Caine 1981). The correct next step is antidepressant treatment and follow-up cognitive assessment.
pearl: Pseudodementia: 'I don't know' with effortful disengagement and preserved alertness — treat the depression first and reassess cognition; scores may fully normalize.
evidence: t_geri.md — Depression can masquerade as cognitive impairment — the pseudodementia presentation (Caine 1981), where patients say 'I don't know' rather than confabulate, show effortful disengagement, and improve cognitively when mood is treated.

stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted following a suicide attempt by acetaminophen overdose. When the student asks about means restriction, he asks only: 'Do you have access to anything dangerous at home?' The patient answers 'no.' The attending asks what a complete means safety assessment requires. Which response is best?
options: A. Ask the patient if he feels safe returning home — a verbal assurance of safety constitutes adequate means restriction documentation. | B. Ask specifically about firearms, stockpiled medications, sharps and ligatures, and who will remove or secure each item — then ask how it will be confirmed before discharge. | C. Have the patient and family sign a no-harm contract — a signed document constitutes the means safety plan. | D. Document 'means safety discussed' in the note — documenting the discussion fulfills the clinical obligation.

stem: A 57-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted through the ED with altered mental status. The nurse establishes IV access and is preparing to infuse D5W. He appears malnourished and confused. Which step must occur before the glucose infusion is started?

stem: A 28-year-old man with opioid use disorder requests buprenorphine. He last used heroin 5 hours ago and reports mild cramping but looks comfortable. His COWS score is 5. He says, 'I'm ready to start — please give it now.' What is the most appropriate response?

stem: A 61-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted for detoxification. On day 2, a nurse pages: he is increasingly confused, stumbling when ambulated, and his eyes appear to be 'moving strangely.' He was ambulatory on admission. Which diagnosis must be excluded immediately?
